title: The pension bill, year by year
question: What does the City employees’ pension fund take in from employers and workers, what does it pay out, and how many workers stand behind each pensioner?
finding: Employers paid $685.3 million into the San Francisco employees’ pension fund in the year to June 2025, against $592.6 million in 2015; the bill peaked at $836.6 million in 2021. Pensions paid out rose from $1.12 billion to $2.00 billion (79% more), and in every one of the 11 years pensions paid were larger than employer and worker contributions together, by $871.9 million in 2025; investment income has to cover that. There were 1.12 working members for each person drawing a pension in 2015 and 1.08 in 2025. By the fund’s own smoothed measure it held 85.6% of what it has promised in 2015 and 96.8% in 2025.
how: Contributions, pensions paid and investment income are the current-year column of the summary table in each year’s audited statements of the San Francisco City and County Employees’ Retirement System (figures printed in thousands). Members, funded share and shortfall are from the summary tables of each July 1 valuation by the fund’s actuary, keyed to the fiscal year that ended the day before. Pensionable pay is the “Annual Pensionable Earnings” line of each valuation; the employer share divides the year’s employer contributions by it. The last three columns are from the City’s payroll file: regular salaries, the “retirement” column (what the City paid toward retirement for each employee) and one divided by the other.
limits: This describes the fund; it is not a warning sign in itself. A mature pension fund normally pays out more than it collects in contributions and relies on investment income. The fund’s 2025 statements say it also covers eligible staff of the school district, the community college district and the Superior Court, and the payroll file covers only employees the City pays, so the fund’s employer contributions and the payroll file’s retirement column are shown side by side and do not have to agree. The “funded” share uses the fund’s smoothed value of its investments and its own assumed return; the market-value share is shown beside it. The fiscal 2015 member counts and funded share come from the prior-year column of the 2016 valuation because no 2015 valuation is published on the fund’s site.
